headline: Canada answers US tariffs with its own, matching them rate for rate on C$27.6 billion of goods
dek: Ottawa's countermeasures take effect on September 8 and cover more than 700 categories of American products. A C$7.5 billion support package for affected workers landed alongside them.
summary: Canada will impose tariffs of 15, 25 and 50 per cent on roughly C$27.6 billion of US goods from September 8, mirroring US rates product by product, after trade talks broke down last week.

image.alt: Stacked shipping containers at a commercial port

body.text: Canada announced on Tuesday that it will impose retaliatory tariffs on about C$27.6 billion — roughly US$19.9 billion — of American goods, matching United States tariff rates product by product. The measures take effect at 12:01 a.m. on September 8. Goods already in transit are exempt.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne set out the approach as "dollar for dollar, rate for rate." Where Washington has put a 50 per cent tariff on a Canadian product, Ottawa's list applies 50 per cent to the equivalent American one; elsewhere the rates are 15 or 25 per cent. According to the Department of Finance's published list, more than 700 categories are covered, including steel, aluminium, furniture, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, plastics and electronics.

The trigger was the collapse of negotiations late last week, after which the United States imposed 50 per cent tariffs on roughly US$20 billion of Canadian goods. Prime Minister Mark Carney had already suspended talks.
When the United States of America asked too much and offered too little, we made a choice. We chose Canada.
body.cite: François-Philippe Champagne, Canadian Finance Minister, via the Associated Press

body.text: Ottawa paired the tariffs with a C$7.5 billion (about US$5.4 billion) package of support for workers and businesses hit by the American measures — an acknowledgment that a retaliatory tariff does not undo the damage of the original one, and that Canadian steel, dairy, appliance and farm-equipment producers are the ones absorbing it.

The costs run in both directions, and it is worth being precise about which is which. Analysts cited by Al Jazeera estimated that American households could face higher prices on around 550 consumer goods **imported from Canada** — a consequence of the United States' own 50 per cent tariff, not of Ottawa's retaliation. Canada's counter-tariffs will raise the price of American goods for Canadian buyers. Estimates put roughly five per cent of Canada's total exports to the United States in the line of fire from the original American duties, though that figure came from unnamed experts and should be read as an estimate rather than a measurement.

President Donald Trump wrote on social media that the United States has lost around US$60 billion a year to Canada over the past decade, and has accused Canada of "ripping off" the United States. Canadian officials frame it differently: Al Jazeera cited Canada's trade surplus with the United States at C$9.9 billion, a figure an order of magnitude smaller than the one the president invoked, in part because the two countries measure and describe the relationship differently — goods alone versus goods and services, and gross flows versus net.
Carney's own framing was sharper than his finance minister's.
You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked.
body.cite: Mark Carney, Prime Minister of Canada, via NPR/AP

body.text: Champagne struck a different note on the same day, telling reporters in remarks carried by NPR and the Associated Press: "It's all about fairness. It's all about level playing field."
Why it reaches ordinary shopping baskets

The Canada–United States relationship is not two economies trading with each other so much as one supply chain drawn across a border. Car parts, food, energy and industrial inputs cross repeatedly before anything reaches a shelf. That is why tariffs in this particular relationship tend to raise costs on both sides rather than shifting them cleanly from one to the other.

Two weeks remain before the Canadian measures take effect. Trump has separately threatened a further round of 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian vehicles, auto parts and steel. Neither government has said whether talks will resume before September 8.

body.title: Reading the numbers
items: The gap between the widely reported "C$27.6 billion" and "about US$20 billion" figures is a currency conversion, not a disagreement — Al Jazeera published both (C$27.6bn = US$19.9bn).
The 550-consumer-products figure describes American prices on Canadian imports under the US tariff. It is an analyst estimate of a future effect, not a measured outcome.
The C$7.5 billion support package is an announced commitment; how it is distributed has not been detailed.

uncertain: Whether the United States will follow through on the threatened additional 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian autos, auto parts and steel before September 8.
Whether either government will return to the table before the measures take effect.
How much of the tariff cost actually reaches consumers on either side. Every figure circulating on this is a projection.
The 'roughly five per cent of exports' estimate, which is attributed to unnamed experts and which we could not trace to a named analyst.
